title: Spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino
summary: Garlic, olive oil and chili, tossed with pasta and its starchy water. Ready in the time it takes to boil the pot.
steps: Bring a large pot of water to the boil and salt it well, so it tastes pleasantly of the sea. Cook the spaghetti until it still has a firm bite in the centre, about 2 minutes less than the packet says, and scoop out a big mug of the cloudy cooking water before you drain.

While the pasta cooks, pour the oil into a wide, cold frying pan and add the sliced garlic. Warm it over low heat so the garlic sizzles gently and turns pale gold, about 4 minutes. Don't let it brown: dark garlic tastes bitter. Stir in the chili flakes for the last few seconds.

Lift the spaghetti straight into the pan with tongs and add a splash of the pasta water. Toss hard over medium heat for a minute or two. The starch in the water and the oil come together into a glossy sauce that clings to every strand, so add more water if it looks dry.
Take the pan off the heat, scatter over the parsley, taste and add salt if needed. Serve straight away, while it's silky.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Shakshuka
summary: Eggs poached in a smoky, spiced tomato and pepper sauce. Bring bread for the pan.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide, deep frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion and pepper for about 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until soft and starting to colour.
Add the garlic, cumin and paprika and stir for a minute, until the spices smell toasty. Don't let them burn, or they turn bitter.
Pour in the tomatoes, crush them with a spoon, season with salt and simmer for about 10 minutes, until the sauce is thick enough to hold a channel when you drag a spoon through it.
Make six little wells in the sauce and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook on low heat for 5 to 7 minutes, until the whites are set but the yolks are still runny.
Scatter over the crumbled feta and coriander and bring the pan to the table, with bread for dipping.
keep: Best eaten fresh, because the eggs and crisp bits don't reheat well. Leftover sauce keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days. Warm it up and cook fresh eggs in it.

title: Red lentil soup
summary: A golden, lemony soup that comes almost entirely from the cupboard.
steps: Melt the butter in a large pot over low heat and cook the onion and carrot gently for about 8 minutes, until soft and sweet but not browned.
Stir in the garlic and cumin and cook for a minute, until fragrant.
Add the rinsed lentils and stock, bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer for about 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the lentils have collapsed into a thick purée.
Blend until smooth, then season with salt and squeeze in lemon juice a little at a time, tasting as you go. The lemon brightens the earthy lentils.
keep: This keeps well: cool it, then store it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. The flavour often gets even better overnight. Reheat gently in a pan until piping hot, adding a splash of water if it has thickened.

title: Chickpea and herb salad
summary: Crunchy, sharp and filling enough for lunch on its own.
steps: Put the sliced onion in a large bowl with the vinegar and a pinch of salt and leave it for 5 minutes. This softens its bite and turns it a pretty pink.
Add the drained chickpeas, diced cucumber and torn parsley and mint.
Pour over the oil, season well with salt and pepper and toss everything together. Taste and add a little more vinegar if it needs more zing.
keep: Salads are best fresh. To keep some, store the undressed ingredients in the fridge for up to 1 day and dress them just before eating. Keep crunchy things like toasted bread or nuts separate until the last minute.

title: Spaghetti alla carbonara
summary: Rome's own: crisp guanciale, egg yolks and pecorino turned into a silky sauce by the heat of the pasta. No cream.
steps: Cut the guanciale into short strips about the thickness of a pencil. Put them in a cold, dry frying pan and cook over medium-low heat, so the fat melts out slowly and the edges turn crisp and golden, about 8 minutes. Take the pan off the heat and keep the fat in it: it's part of the sauce.
In a bowl, whisk the egg yolks with most of the pecorino and a generous grinding of black pepper until you have a thick, sunny paste.
Cook the spaghetti in well-salted boiling water until al dente, and save a mug of the cooking water before draining.

Tip the spaghetti into the guanciale pan, still off the heat, and toss to coat it in the fat. Let it sit for 30 seconds so it's hot but not scorching, then add the yolk mixture and a splash of pasta water.

Toss quickly and keep everything moving, adding more water a spoonful at a time, until the eggs thicken into a creamy, glossy sauce. If the pan is too hot the eggs will scramble, so go slowly. Serve at once with the rest of the pecorino and more pepper.
keep: These egg and cheese sauces are at their best straight from the pan. Leftovers keep in the fridge for up to 1 day. Reheat gently in a pan with a splash of water, stirring, so the sauce turns creamy again.

title: Bucatini all'amatriciana
summary: From the town of Amatrice: guanciale, tomato and pecorino, with a little heat from dried chili.
steps: Cut the guanciale into thick strips and render it slowly in a wide pan over medium-low heat, until the fat runs and the strips turn golden, about 8 minutes. Crumble in the chili and let it sizzle for a few seconds.
Pour in the wine and let it bubble for a minute or two, scraping the bottom of the pan, until the sharp smell of alcohol fades.

Lift out the guanciale with a slotted spoon and set it aside so it stays crisp. Add the tomatoes to the fat, crush them with a wooden spoon and simmer for about 15 minutes, until the sauce is thick and glossy.
Meanwhile, cook the bucatini in salted boiling water until al dente. Drain, keeping a little of the water.
Stir the guanciale back into the sauce, add the pasta and toss over the heat for a minute, loosening with pasta water if needed. Take it off the heat, add the pecorino, toss again and serve.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Risotto alla milanese
summary: Saffron-gold risotto from Milan, finished with butter and Parmigiano. Classic beside ossobuco.
steps: Crumble the saffron threads into a ladle of the hot stock and leave them to steep, so they release their colour and aroma. Keep the rest of the stock at a gentle simmer on the back of the stove.
Melt half the butter in a wide, heavy pan over low heat and cook the onion slowly for about 5 minutes, until soft and translucent but not browned.
Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes, until the grains look glassy at the edges and feel hot to the touch. This toasting helps them hold their shape.
Pour in the wine and stir until it has almost all evaporated.

Add a ladle of hot stock and stir until it's mostly absorbed, then add the next. Keep going for 16 to 18 minutes, stirring often, and add the saffron stock halfway through. The risotto is ready when the rice is tender with a slight bite and the texture is loose and creamy.
Off the heat, beat in the remaining cold butter and the Parmigiano. Cover and rest for 2 minutes, then serve: it should spread slowly across the plate in a wave.
keep: Cool risotto quickly, within an hour, then keep it covered in the fridge and eat it within 1 day. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of stock until piping hot, or roll it into balls, coat in breadcrumbs and fry as arancini.

title: Trofie al pesto genovese
summary: Basil pounded with garlic, pine nuts and two cheeses, the way Genoa makes it. A mortar gives the best texture.
ingredients: 70 ml mild extra virgin olive oil
steps: Put the garlic and a pinch of coarse salt in a large mortar and pound them into a creamy paste. Add the pine nuts and keep working until smooth.

Add the basil a handful at a time. Instead of beating, press and grind the leaves against the side of the mortar in a circular motion. This crushes them gently and keeps the pesto bright green instead of dark and bitter.
Stir in both cheeses, then pour in the oil in a thin stream, mixing as you go, until the pesto is thick but spoonable.
Cook the trofie in salted boiling water until al dente, and keep a little of the water.
Drain the pasta and toss it in a bowl with the pesto and a spoonful of cooking water to loosen it. Don't put the pesto over heat, or the basil will darken and lose its fresh flavour.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Parmigiana di melanzane
summary: Layers of fried aubergine, tomato sauce, mozzarella and Parmigiano, baked until bubbling. Even better the next day.
ingredients: 300 g fior di latte mozzarella, diced
steps: Slice the aubergines lengthways about 5 mm thick, sprinkle them with salt and leave them in a colander for an hour. This draws out bitter juices and stops them soaking up too much oil. Pat the slices dry with kitchen paper.
Meanwhile, warm the olive oil with the garlic, add the passata and a few basil leaves, and simmer gently for 20 minutes until slightly thickened. Season with salt.
Heat the sunflower oil in a deep pan and fry the aubergine slices in batches until golden on both sides. Drain them on kitchen paper.

Heat the oven to 200°C. Spread a little sauce in a baking dish, then add a layer of aubergine, more sauce, mozzarella, Parmigiano and torn basil. Repeat until everything is used, finishing with sauce and a good layer of Parmigiano.
Bake for about 40 minutes, until bubbling at the edges and golden on top. Let it rest for at least 20 minutes before cutting, so the layers set and slice cleanly.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. It often slices even better the next day. Reheat portions in the oven at 180°C, covered with foil, for about 20 minutes, until hot in the middle.

title: Tiramisù
summary: Coffee-soaked savoiardi between layers of mascarpone cream. Needs about 4 hours in the fridge to set.
steps: Separate the eggs. Whisk the yolks with half the sugar until pale, thick and doubled in volume, then add the mascarpone and beat gently until smooth and creamy.

In a very clean bowl, whisk the whites with the remaining sugar until they hold firm, glossy peaks. Fold them into the mascarpone in two or three batches with a spatula and a light hand, so you keep the air in.
Pour the cooled espresso into a shallow dish. Dip each savoiardo in it for about a second on each side: long enough to soak the outside, not so long that it falls apart. Lay them snugly in your dish.
Spread half the cream over the biscuits, add another layer of dipped savoiardi, then cover with the rest of the cream and smooth the top.
Cover and chill for at least 4 hours, or overnight, so the biscuits soften and the flavours settle. Dust generously with cocoa just before serving.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. Dairy-rich and set desserts shouldn't sit at room temperature for long.

title: Oyakodon
summary: Chicken and egg simmered in sweet dashi and poured over rice. The name means parent and child.
steps: Put the dashi, soy sauce, mirin and sugar in a small frying pan with the sliced onion and simmer for about 3 minutes, until the onion softens.
Add the chicken pieces in one layer and simmer for 5 to 6 minutes, turning once, until cooked through.
Beat the eggs lightly with chopsticks so that streaks of white remain. Pour about two thirds over the chicken, cover and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the rest of the egg and cook for 30 seconds more, until it's just set but still soft and silky.
Slide everything, with the sauce, over bowls of hot rice and scatter with spring onion.
keep: Cool rice dishes quickly, within an hour, then keep them covered in the fridge and eat them within 1 day. Reheat until piping hot all the way through, adding a splash of water so the rice doesn't dry out.

title: Okonomiyaki
summary: Osaka's savoury cabbage pancake, topped with pork belly, sweet sauce, mayonnaise and bonito flakes that wave in the heat.
ingredients: Okonomiyaki sauce, Japanese mayonnaise, aonori and katsuobushi, to top
steps: Whisk the flour and dashi into a smooth batter, then beat in the eggs.
Fold in the shredded cabbage and spring onions until everything is just coated. Don't overmix: the air in the batter keeps the pancake light.
Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat and spread half the mixture into a thick round about 2 cm high. Lay two slices of pork belly on top.
Cook for about 5 minutes, until golden underneath, then flip carefully with two spatulas and cook for 5 minutes more with the pork side down, until crisp. Repeat with the rest.
Brush the top with okonomiyaki sauce, zigzag with mayonnaise and scatter with aonori and katsuobushi. The bonito flakes will wave in the heat.
keep: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat gently until piping hot all the way through, covered so it doesn't dry out.

title: Chicken karaage
summary: Ginger-and-soy marinated chicken, coated in potato starch and fried twice for a thin, shattering crust.
ingredients: 500 g chicken thigh, in large bite-sized pieces
steps: Cut the chicken into large bite-sized pieces and mix it with the soy sauce, sake, ginger and garlic. Leave it to marinate for 20 minutes.
Drain off any excess marinade and toss the pieces in the potato starch, pressing it on so every piece is well coated.
Heat the oil to 170°C and fry the chicken in batches for about 3 minutes, until pale golden. Lift it onto a rack and rest for 4 minutes: the heat carries on cooking the inside.
Turn the oil up to 190°C and fry the chicken again for about 1 minute, until deep golden and very crisp.
Drain on kitchen paper and serve straight away with lemon wedges.
keep: These are best eaten fresh, while they're crisp. Leftovers keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 day. Reheat them on a tray in a hot oven (200°C) for 8 to 10 minutes to crisp them up again, rather than in the microwave.

title: Miso soup with tofu and wakame
summary: The everyday soup of Japanese home cooking. Good dashi matters, and the miso should never boil.
ingredients: 150 g silken tofu, in small cubes
steps: Soak the dried wakame in cold water for 5 minutes, until it swells, then drain it.
Bring the dashi to a gentle simmer and add the tofu cubes and wakame.
Turn the heat to low. Put the miso in a ladle, dip it into the pot and stir with chopsticks until the miso dissolves, then stir it into the soup.
Heat until steaming, without letting it boil: boiling dulls the flavour of the miso. Serve topped with spring onion.
keep: This keeps well: cool it, then store it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. The flavour often gets even better overnight. Reheat gently in a pan until piping hot, adding a splash of water if it has thickened.

title: Nikujaga
summary: Beef and potatoes simmered in sweet soy dashi until the potatoes soak up the broth. Japanese comfort food.
steps: Heat the oil in a pot and fry the beef until it just changes colour. Add the onion, potatoes and carrot and stir to coat them in the fat.
Pour in the dashi and sake, bring to a boil and skim off any foam that rises.
Add the mirin and sugar. Lay a small lid or a circle of baking paper directly on the surface so the liquid circulates over the vegetables, and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the soy sauce and simmer for 10 minutes more, until the potatoes are tender and the broth has reduced by about half. Adding the soy later keeps the potatoes from firming up.
Blanch the snow peas for a minute and scatter them over just before serving.
keep: This keeps well: cool it, then store it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. The flavour often gets even better overnight. Reheat gently in a pan until piping hot, adding a splash of water if it has thickened.

title: Bruschetta al pomodoro
summary: Grilled country bread rubbed with garlic and piled with ripe tomato, basil and good olive oil.
steps: Dice the tomatoes and put them in a bowl with a good pinch of salt, the oil and torn basil, then leave them for 10 minutes. The salt draws out the juices, which mix with the oil into a light dressing.
Toast or grill the bread over high heat until it's crisp outside and charred at the edges, but still a little soft in the middle.
While the bread is hot, rub one side of each slice with the cut garlic. The rough surface works like a grater, so a few strokes are enough.
Spoon the tomatoes and some of their juices on top just before serving, so the bread stays crunchy.
keep: Best made just before serving. The tomato topping keeps covered in the fridge for up to 1 day; toast fresh bread and assemble at the last minute.

title: Insalata caprese
summary: Mozzarella, tomato and basil in the colours of the Italian flag. Only worth making with ripe summer tomatoes.
steps: Take the mozzarella and tomatoes out of the fridge 30 minutes before you start, so they lose their chill and taste of more.
Slice both about 1 cm thick. Drain the mozzarella slices briefly on kitchen paper so they don't water down the plate.
Overlap the tomato and mozzarella slices on a platter, tucking basil leaves between them.
Season with salt and a pinch of oregano, and finish with a generous drizzle of your best olive oil. Serve at room temperature.
keep: Salads are best fresh. To keep some, store the undressed ingredients in the fridge for up to 1 day and dress them just before eating. Keep crunchy things like toasted bread or nuts separate until the last minute.

title: Arancini al ragù
summary: Golden fried rice balls with a heart of meat ragù, peas and melting cheese. Cook the rice a day ahead.
steps: The day before, cook the rice in the stock with the saffron until the liquid is absorbed and the rice is tender. Stir in the butter and cheese, spread it on a tray and let it cool completely. Cold rice holds its shape far better.

Wet your hands and take a handful of rice. Flatten it in your palm, press a hollow in the middle and fill it with a spoonful of ragù, a few peas and a cube of provola. Close the rice around the filling and shape it into a ball.
Whisk the flour with enough cold water to make a smooth, thin batter. Dip each ball in the batter, then roll it in breadcrumbs until fully coated.

Heat the oil to 170°C and fry a few at a time for about 4 minutes, turning, until deep golden all over. Drain on kitchen paper and wait a couple of minutes before eating, because the cheese inside gets very hot.
keep: These are best eaten fresh, while they're crisp. Leftovers keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 day. Reheat them on a tray in a hot oven (200°C) for 8 to 10 minutes to crisp them up again, rather than in the microwave.

title: Supplì
summary: Rome's street snack: tomato risotto croquettes with a string of mozzarella that stretches as you bite.
steps: Cook the rice with the passata, adding hot stock a ladle at a time as it's absorbed, until just tender, about 18 minutes. Stir in the Parmigiano, spread it on a tray and let it cool completely.
Take a heaped tablespoon of rice, press a stick of mozzarella into the middle and close the rice around it, shaping a neat oval about the size of an egg.
Dip each one in beaten egg, then roll it in breadcrumbs. For an extra-crisp crust, repeat the egg and crumbs once more.
Fry at 170°C for 3 to 4 minutes until crisp and golden. Serve hot, so when you pull one apart the mozzarella stretches into a long string.
keep: These are best eaten fresh, while they're crisp. Leftovers keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 day. Reheat them on a tray in a hot oven (200°C) for 8 to 10 minutes to crisp them up again, rather than in the microwave.

title: Panzanella
summary: A Tuscan bread salad that turns stale bread into lunch with tomatoes, cucumber, red onion and basil.
steps: Tear the bread into chunks and soak it in cold water for about 5 minutes, until soft. Squeeze it firmly to remove as much water as possible, then crumble it into a large bowl.
Chop the tomatoes and cucumber into bite-sized pieces and add them to the bread with their juices and the sliced onion.
Dress with the oil, vinegar and a good pinch of salt, tear in the basil and toss with your hands so the bread soaks up the tomato juices.
Leave it for 20 minutes before serving. The salad gets better as the flavours mingle.
keep: Salads are best fresh. To keep some, store the undressed ingredients in the fridge for up to 1 day and dress them just before eating. Keep crunchy things like toasted bread or nuts separate until the last minute.

title: Crostini toscani
summary: Chicken liver pâté on toasted bread, the first thing on the table at a Tuscan Sunday lunch.
ingredients: 60 ml vin santo or dry white wine
steps: Warm the oil and soften the onion over medium heat for 5 minutes. Add the chicken livers and cook, turning, until browned outside but still a little pink inside, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the wine and let it bubble, then add the anchovies and capers and cook for 10 minutes more, stirring, until the anchovies melt into the sauce.
Take it off the heat and chop everything finely on a board, or pulse it briefly with the butter, keeping some texture.
Toast the bread slices, spread them with the warm pâté and serve straight away.
keep: Keep the pâté in a covered container in the fridge for up to 2 days and toast fresh bread when you serve it.

title: Prosciutto e melone
summary: Sweet cantaloupe draped with salty Parma ham. No cooking, just good ingredients.
steps: Choose a melon that feels heavy for its size and smells sweet at the stem end. Chill it for an hour if you have time.
Halve the melon, scoop out the seeds and cut it into wedges, then slice away the rind.
Drape a thin slice of prosciutto over each wedge, letting it fall in loose folds.
Finish with a twist of black pepper and serve cold.
keep: Best served fresh. Cut melon keeps covered in the fridge for 1 day; add the prosciutto just before serving.

title: Fiori di zucca fritti
summary: Courgette flowers stuffed with mozzarella and anchovy, fried in a light, crisp batter.
steps: Open each flower gently and pinch out the pistil inside. Check for insects and give them a gentle shake rather than a wash, so they stay dry.
Tuck a stick of mozzarella and a piece of anchovy inside each flower and twist the tips of the petals to close it.
Just before frying, whisk the flour with the ice-cold sparkling water into a thin batter. Cold, bubbly water makes the coating light and crisp.
Heat the oil to 175°C. Dip each flower in the batter, let the excess drip off and fry for about 2 minutes until pale gold. Drain, sprinkle with salt and serve straight away.
keep: These are best eaten fresh, while they're crisp. Leftovers keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 day. Reheat them on a tray in a hot oven (200°C) for 8 to 10 minutes to crisp them up again, rather than in the microwave.

title: Frittata di zucchine
summary: A thick, golden omelette with courgettes and Parmigiano. Good warm or cold, cut into squares.
steps: Warm the oil in a 24 cm non-stick pan and cook the onion and courgettes over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, until soft and lightly golden.
Beat the eggs with the Parmigiano, torn basil, salt and pepper, and pour them over the vegetables. Stir once to spread everything evenly.
Turn the heat to low, cover and cook for about 8 minutes, until the edges are set and the top is almost firm.
Slide the frittata onto a plate, flip it back into the pan and cook for 2 minutes more to set the other side. Serve warm or at room temperature, cut into wedges.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. It's lovely cold or at room temperature, cut into squares for lunch or a picnic.

title: Cacio e pepe
summary: Just pecorino, black pepper and pasta water whisked into a creamy sauce. Three ingredients, one technique.
steps: Crush the peppercorns coarsely and toast them in a dry, wide pan for a minute, until fragrant. Once the pasta water is boiling, add a ladle of it to the pepper and let it simmer.
In a bowl, mix the finely grated pecorino with a few spoonfuls of warm, not boiling, pasta water and mash it into a smooth, thick cream. Water that's too hot makes the cheese clump.
Cook the pasta until quite al dente and lift it into the pepper pan with a little more water. Toss for a minute so it finishes cooking.
Take the pan off the heat, wait a few seconds, then add the pecorino cream and toss quickly, adding water a little at a time, until the sauce is creamy and glossy. Serve straight away.
keep: These egg and cheese sauces are at their best straight from the pan. Leftovers keep in the fridge for up to 1 day. Reheat gently in a pan with a splash of water, stirring, so the sauce turns creamy again.

title: Rigatoni alla gricia
summary: The ancestor of carbonara and amatriciana: crisp guanciale, pecorino and pepper. No egg, no tomato.
steps: Cut the guanciale into strips and render it slowly in a wide pan over medium-low heat, until the fat runs clear and the pieces are crisp and golden.
Cook the rigatoni in salted water until al dente, then lift them into the guanciale pan with a generous ladle of the starchy cooking water.
Toss over low heat for a minute so the fat and water start to come together, then take the pan off the heat.
Add the pecorino a handful at a time, tossing and adding a splash of water if needed, until the sauce turns creamy. Finish with plenty of black pepper.
keep: These egg and cheese sauces are at their best straight from the pan. Leftovers keep in the fridge for up to 1 day. Reheat gently in a pan with a splash of water, stirring, so the sauce turns creamy again.

title: Penne all'arrabbiata
summary: Penne in a garlicky tomato sauce with as much chili as you dare. Arrabbiata means angry.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pan over low heat with the garlic and crumbled chili, until the garlic sizzles gently and smells sweet but hasn't browned.
Add the tomatoes, crush them with a wooden spoon and simmer for about 12 minutes, until the sauce is thick and the oil starts to separate at the edges. Season with salt.
Cook the penne in salted water until al dente, drain and toss them in the sauce over the heat for a minute.
Scatter over the parsley and serve. Taste first: if you want it angrier, add more chili.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Lasagne alla bolognese
summary: Layers of egg pasta, slow-cooked ragù, béchamel and Parmigiano. Make the ragù the day before.
steps: Heat the oven to 180°C and butter a deep baking dish. Warm the ragù and béchamel slightly so they spread easily.
Spread a thin layer of ragù on the bottom, then add a layer of pasta sheets, slightly overlapping. Spoon over ragù, then béchamel, and sprinkle with Parmigiano.
Repeat the layers 5 or 6 times, finishing with béchamel, a generous handful of Parmigiano and a few flakes of butter.
Bake for about 40 minutes, until the top is golden and the edges bubble. Rest for 15 minutes before cutting so the layers hold together.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. It often slices even better the next day. Reheat portions in the oven at 180°C, covered with foil, for about 20 minutes, until hot in the middle.

title: Tagliatelle al ragù
summary: Bologna's own ragù of beef and pork with a little tomato and milk, on ribbons of egg pasta. Low and slow.
steps: Warm a little oil in a heavy pot and cook the pancetta with the chopped carrot, celery and onion over low heat for about 10 minutes, until soft and sweet.
Turn up the heat, add the beef and pork and cook, breaking up the meat, until it's well browned and any liquid has evaporated. Browning builds much of the flavour.
Pour in the wine and let it bubble away, then stir in the passata and milk. The milk makes the meat tender and the sauce mellow.

Turn the heat right down and simmer, partly covered, for 2½ to 3 hours, stirring now and then and adding a splash of water if it gets too dry. The ragù is ready when it's thick, glossy and deep in colour.
Cook the tagliatelle, toss them with the ragù and a little pasta water, and serve with grated Parmigiano.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Spaghetti alle vongole
summary: Clams opened in white wine and garlic, tossed with spaghetti in their briny juices. Naples on a plate.
steps: Soak the clams in cold salted water for an hour so they spit out any sand, then rinse them. Throw away any that are cracked or stay open when tapped.
Warm the oil with the garlic and chili in a wide pan. Add the clams and wine, cover and cook over high heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking the pan, until the shells open. Discard any that stay closed.
Meanwhile, cook the spaghetti until 2 minutes short of al dente.
Add the spaghetti to the clam pan and toss over the heat for 2 minutes, so the pasta finishes cooking in the briny juices and soaks up their flavour.
Toss in the parsley and serve right away, with a bowl on the table for the shells.
keep: Seafood is best eaten the day it's cooked. If you have leftovers, cool them quickly, keep them covered in the fridge and eat them within 1 day, reheating gently.

title: Pasta alla Norma
summary: Catania's pasta with fried aubergine, tomato sauce, basil and grated salted ricotta.
steps: Fry the aubergine cubes in batches in plenty of hot oil until deep golden and soft inside. Drain on kitchen paper and sprinkle with salt.
In another pan, warm a little oil with the garlic, add the passata and simmer for 15 minutes until slightly thickened. Season.
Stir most of the aubergine and a few torn basil leaves into the sauce, keeping some aubergine back for the top.
Cook the pasta, toss it with the sauce, and serve topped with the remaining aubergine, more basil and a generous grating of ricotta salata.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Gnocchi alla sorrentina
summary: Potato gnocchi baked in tomato sauce with mozzarella and basil until bubbling.
steps: Simmer the passata with the oil, garlic and a few basil leaves for 15 minutes, until it thickens slightly. Season with salt.
Heat the oven to 220°C. Cook the gnocchi in salted boiling water and lift them out as soon as they float to the surface.
Mix the gnocchi with the sauce and half the mozzarella and spread them in a baking dish.
Scatter over the remaining mozzarella and the Parmigiano and bake for about 10 minutes, until the cheese is melted and bubbling. Finish with fresh basil.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. It often slices even better the next day. Reheat portions in the oven at 180°C, covered with foil, for about 20 minutes, until hot in the middle.

title: Orecchiette con cime di rapa
summary: Puglia's ear-shaped pasta cooked with bitter turnip greens, garlic, anchovy and chili.
ingredients: 800 g cime di rapa or broccoli rabe
steps: Trim the cime di rapa, keeping the tender leaves and florets. Bring a big pot of salted water to the boil, add the greens and cook for 4 minutes, then add the orecchiette to the same pot.
Meanwhile, warm the oil in a large pan with the garlic, chili and anchovies, stirring until the anchovies melt into the oil.
When the pasta is al dente, drain it with the greens and tip everything into the anchovy pan. Toss well so the greens break down a little and coat the pasta.
Serve topped with the toasted breadcrumbs, which add crunch in place of cheese.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Pasta e fagioli
summary: A thick, creamy soup of beans and small pasta. Farmhouse food that warms you through.
steps: Warm the oil in a pot and cook the onion, carrot and celery gently for 8 to 10 minutes, until soft. Stir in the tomato paste and rosemary and cook for a minute.
Add the beans and stock, bring to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes so the flavours come together.
Blend about a third of the soup and stir it back in. This makes it thick and creamy without any cream.
Add the pasta and simmer, stirring often so it doesn't stick, until tender. Rest for 5 minutes off the heat and serve with a drizzle of olive oil.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Saltimbocca alla romana
summary: Veal escalopes topped with prosciutto and sage, pan-fried in butter and white wine. The name means jump in the mouth.
steps: If the escalopes are thick, flatten them between two sheets of baking paper. Lay a slice of prosciutto and a sage leaf on each and fix them with a toothpick.
Dust only the underside with flour and shake off the excess.
Melt the butter in a wide pan until it foams. Fry the escalopes ham side up for 2 minutes, then flip and cook for 1 minute more, until the ham is crisp.
Move the meat to a warm plate, pour the wine into the pan and let it bubble, scraping up the brown bits, until it reduces to a glossy sauce. Spoon it over the saltimbocca and serve.
keep: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat gently until piping hot all the way through, covered so it doesn't dry out.

title: Pollo alla cacciatora
summary: Hunter's-style chicken braised with tomatoes, olives, rosemary and wine until it falls off the bone.
steps: Season the chicken and brown it well in the oil over medium-high heat, skin side down first, until golden all over. Set it aside.
Lower the heat, add the onion and garlic to the same pan and cook for 5 minutes until soft. Pour in the wine and let it bubble for a couple of minutes, scraping the bottom.
Add the tomatoes, olives and rosemary, crush the tomatoes, and nestle the chicken back in.
Cover and simmer gently for about 45 minutes, until the chicken is tender and the sauce has thickened. Serve with bread or polenta.
keep: This keeps well: cool it, then store it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. The flavour often gets even better overnight. Reheat gently in a pan until piping hot, adding a splash of water if it has thickened.

title: Ossobuco alla milanese
summary: Braised veal shanks finished with gremolata, the classic partner to saffron risotto.
steps: With scissors, snip the thin membrane around each shank in two or three places so they don't curl as they cook. Season, dust with flour and brown them well in the butter on both sides.
Add the onion and cook until soft, then pour in the wine and let it reduce by half.
Add the stock, cover and simmer very gently for about 1½ hours, turning the shanks once, until the meat is tender enough to cut with a spoon. Add a splash of water if the sauce gets too thick.
Finely chop the lemon zest, garlic and parsley together to make the gremolata and scatter it over just before serving. Don't forget the marrow in the bone.
keep: This keeps well: cool it, then store it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. The flavour often gets even better overnight. Reheat gently in a pan until piping hot, adding a splash of water if it has thickened.

title: Cotoletta alla milanese
summary: A bone-in veal chop, breaded and fried in clarified butter until deep golden. Serve with lemon.
ingredients: 2 veal chops on the bone, 2 cm thick
steps: Pound the meat lightly to an even thickness, leaving the bone attached, and season it with a little salt.
Dip the chops in beaten egg, then press them firmly into the breadcrumbs on both sides so the coating sticks well.
Heat the clarified butter in a wide pan over medium heat and fry the chops for about 4 minutes per side, until deep golden and crisp.
Drain briefly on kitchen paper, sprinkle with salt and serve with lemon wedges.
keep: These are best eaten fresh, while they're crisp. Leftovers keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 day. Reheat them on a tray in a hot oven (200°C) for 8 to 10 minutes to crisp them up again, rather than in the microwave.

title: Polpette al sugo
summary: Soft beef and pork meatballs simmered in tomato sauce. In Italy they come with bread, not spaghetti.
ingredients: 80 g stale bread, soaked in milk
steps: Squeeze the soaked bread well and put it in a bowl with the meat, egg, Parmigiano, garlic, parsley and a good pinch of salt. Mix with your hands until evenly combined, but don't overwork it.
Roll into balls about the size of a walnut, with slightly wet hands so the mixture doesn't stick.
Brown the meatballs in the oil in a wide pan, turning them gently, then pour in the passata.
Cover and simmer gently for 30 minutes, shaking the pan now and then. Serve with plenty of bread for the sauce.
keep: This keeps well: cool it, then store it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. The flavour often gets even better overnight. Reheat gently in a pan until piping hot, adding a splash of water if it has thickened.

title: Scaloppine al limone
summary: Thin veal slices dusted in flour and finished in a buttery lemon sauce. Dinner in 20 minutes.
steps: Pound the escalopes thin and dust them lightly with flour.
Heat the butter and oil in a wide pan until foaming and fry the veal for about 1 minute per side, until lightly golden. Move it to a plate.
Pour the lemon juice and stock into the pan and scrape up the browned bits. Let it bubble for a minute.
Return the veal and its juices and turn it for a minute, until coated in a silky sauce. Scatter with parsley and serve.
keep: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat gently until piping hot all the way through, covered so it doesn't dry out.

title: Orata al forno con patate
summary: Whole sea bream roasted on a bed of potatoes with cherry tomatoes, olives and herbs.
ingredients: 2 sea bream, about 400 g each, cleaned
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C. Toss the potatoes with half the oil, the garlic, rosemary and salt, spread them in a roasting tin and roast for 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, season the fish inside and out and stuff each one with lemon slices and herbs.
Lay the fish on the potatoes with the tomatoes and olives around them, and drizzle with the rest of the oil.
Roast for 20 to 25 minutes, until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily from the bone.
keep: Seafood is best eaten the day it's cooked. If you have leftovers, cool them quickly, keep them covered in the fridge and eat them within 1 day, reheating gently.

title: Bistecca alla fiorentina
summary: A thick T-bone grilled over fierce heat and served rare with olive oil and salt. Tuscany's pride.
ingredients: 1 T-bone steak, about 1.2 kg and 5 cm thick
steps: Take the steak out of the fridge 2 hours before cooking so it comes up to room temperature.
Heat a grill or heavy pan until smoking hot. Cook the steak for 5 minutes per side without moving it, so it forms a dark crust.
Stand the steak upright on its bone for 5 minutes more, which warms the centre without overcooking the outside.
Rest for 5 minutes, cut the meat off the bone and slice it thickly. Season with coarse salt, pepper and a drizzle of olive oil.
keep: Keep leftover steak wrapped in the fridge for up to 2 days. Slice it thinly and eat it cold, or warm it very briefly in a hot pan so it doesn't cook further.

title: Salsiccia e friarielli
summary: Pork sausages with bitter Neapolitan greens sautéed in garlic and chili.
steps: Put the sausages in a pan with a splash of water and cook over medium heat. When the water has evaporated, let them fry in their own fat, turning, until browned and cooked through.
Trim the greens, discarding the tough stems, and wash them well.
Warm the oil with the garlic and chili in a large pan, add the greens, cover and cook for about 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until tender.
Add the sausages to the greens for the last 5 minutes so the flavours mingle, then serve.
keep: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat gently until piping hot all the way through, covered so it doesn't dry out.

title: Patate al forno
summary: Crisp roast potatoes with rosemary and garlic, the side that goes with everything.
steps: Heat the oven to 210°C. Cut the potatoes into chunks, then dry them well with a tea towel: dry potatoes crisp, wet ones steam.
Toss them in a roasting tin with the oil, unpeeled garlic, rosemary and salt, and spread them out in a single layer.
Roast for 40 to 45 minutes, turning once halfway, until deep golden and crisp outside and fluffy inside.
keep: Keep them covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat on a tray in a hot oven (220°C) for about 10 minutes so they crisp up again; the microwave makes them soft.

title: Peperonata
summary: Sweet peppers stewed slowly with onion and tomato until soft and jammy.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pan and soften the onion over medium heat for 5 minutes.
Add the peppers and cook for 10 minutes, stirring, until they start to soften and colour at the edges.
Add the tomatoes, cover and simmer gently for about 25 minutes, until everything is soft and jammy.
Stir in a splash of vinegar and torn basil and season with salt. It's lovely warm or at room temperature.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 3 days; it tastes even better the next day. Serve it at room temperature or gently warmed.

title: Caponata
summary: Sicily's sweet and sour aubergine stew with celery, olives, capers and pine nuts.
steps: Fry the aubergine cubes in hot oil in batches until golden, then drain them on kitchen paper.
Blanch the celery in boiling water for 2 minutes, so it softens but stays crunchy.
In a wide pan, soften the onion in a little oil, then add the passata, celery, olives, capers and pine nuts and cook for 10 minutes.
Stir in the vinegar and sugar and let it bubble for a minute, then fold in the aubergine and leave to cool. Caponata tastes best the next day, at room temperature.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 3 days; it tastes even better the next day. Serve it at room temperature or gently warmed.

title: Carciofi alla romana
summary: Whole artichokes braised with mint, garlic and olive oil until meltingly tender.
steps: Pull away the tough outer leaves of each artichoke until you reach the pale, tender ones. Trim the stem and cut off the spiky tip, then rub everything with lemon so it doesn't darken.
Finely chop the mint and garlic with a pinch of salt and push the mixture between the leaves.
Stand the artichokes head down in a pot just big enough to hold them snugly, and pour in the oil and water.
Cover and cook on low heat for 35 to 40 minutes, until a knife slides easily into the base. Serve warm, with the cooking juices spooned over.
keep: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat gently until piping hot all the way through, covered so it doesn't dry out.

title: Fagiolini al pomodoro
summary: Green beans simmered in a garlicky tomato sauce until tender. Simple and very Italian.
steps: Blanch the beans in salted boiling water for 4 minutes, then drain.
Warm the garlic in the oil, add the passata and simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the beans and cook for 10 to 15 minutes, until tender and coated in sauce.
Season and finish with torn basil.
keep: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat gently until piping hot all the way through, covered so it doesn't dry out.

title: Zucchine trifolate
summary: Courgette coins sautéed with garlic and parsley. Ready in minutes.
steps: Warm the oil with the garlic in a wide pan over medium heat until fragrant.
Add the courgettes and cook for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until tender and lightly golden. Don't crowd the pan, or they'll turn watery.
Season with salt and pepper and toss with the parsley.
keep: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat gently until piping hot all the way through, covered so it doesn't dry out.

title: Insalata di finocchi e arance
summary: Crisp fennel and juicy orange with black olives. A bright winter salad from Sicily.
steps: Trim the fennel and slice it as thinly as you can. A mandoline helps.
Cut the peel and white pith off the oranges with a knife, then slice them into rounds, saving any juice.
Arrange the fennel, oranges, onion and olives on a plate, season with salt and pepper, and drizzle with the oil and the saved orange juice.
keep: Salads are best fresh. To keep some, store the undressed ingredients in the fridge for up to 1 day and dress them just before eating. Keep crunchy things like toasted bread or nuts separate until the last minute.

title: Fagioli all'uccelletto
summary: White beans simmered with tomato, garlic and sage. The traditional partner for Tuscan sausages.
steps: Warm the oil with the garlic and sage over low heat, until the leaves crisp and the oil smells fragrant.
Add the tomatoes, crush them and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the beans and simmer for 15 minutes more, stirring now and then, until thick and creamy.
Season with pepper and finish with a drizzle of oil.
keep: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat gently until piping hot all the way through, covered so it doesn't dry out.

title: Melanzane a funghetto
summary: Aubergine cubes fried, then tossed with cherry tomatoes and basil, cooked the way mushrooms are.
steps: Fry the aubergine cubes in hot oil until golden on all sides, then drain on kitchen paper and salt them.
In a clean pan, warm a little oil with the garlic, add the tomatoes and cook for about 5 minutes, until they burst.
Add the aubergine and basil and toss gently for 2 minutes, until everything is coated.
keep: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat gently until piping hot all the way through, covered so it doesn't dry out.

title: Panna cotta
summary: Silky set cream with vanilla and a sharp berry sauce. Needs 4 hours in the fridge to set.
steps: Soak the gelatine leaves in cold water for 10 minutes, until soft.
Heat the cream, milk and sugar with the vanilla seeds and pod until steaming, without letting it boil. Take it off the heat and remove the pod.
Squeeze the gelatine and stir it into the warm cream until completely dissolved. Pour into moulds or glasses and chill for at least 4 hours, until set with a gentle wobble.
For the sauce, simmer the berries with the sugar for 5 minutes, then cool. Dip each mould briefly in hot water, turn out the panna cotta and spoon the sauce over.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. Dairy-rich and set desserts shouldn't sit at room temperature for long.

title: Cannoli siciliani
summary: Crisp fried pastry tubes filled with sweet sheep's ricotta, chocolate and candied orange.
steps: Knead the flour, sugar, lard, egg and Marsala into a firm, smooth dough. Wrap it and rest for an hour.
Roll the dough very thin, cut 10 cm rounds and wrap each around a metal tube, sealing the overlap with a little egg white.
Fry at 180°C for 1 to 2 minutes until blistered and golden. Cool slightly, then slide them off the tubes.
Beat the drained ricotta with the icing sugar until smooth, then fold in the chocolate and orange peel. Pipe it into the shells just before serving, so they stay crisp.
keep: Store the shells and the filling separately: shells in an airtight tin at room temperature, filling covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. Fill them just before serving so the shells stay crisp.

title: Affogato al caffè
summary: A scoop of vanilla gelato drowned in a shot of hot espresso. The quickest dessert in Italy.
steps: Chill the glasses in the freezer for 10 minutes so the gelato doesn't melt too fast.
Put a scoop of gelato in each glass.
Brew the espresso and pour it over the gelato at the table. Scatter with chocolate and eat straight away.
keep: This one doesn't keep. Make it just before you want to eat it.

title: Crostata di marmellata
summary: A shortcrust tart filled with jam under a pastry lattice. Italy's favourite home bake.
steps: Rub the cold butter into the flour until it looks like breadcrumbs, then add the sugar, zest, egg and yolk and bring it together into a dough without kneading too much. Wrap and chill for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 180°C. Roll out two thirds of the pastry and line a 24 cm tart tin.
Spread the jam evenly over the base. Roll out the remaining pastry, cut it into strips and lay them on top in a lattice, pressing the ends onto the edge.
Bake for about 35 minutes, until golden. Let it cool completely before slicing, so the jam sets.
keep: Keep it covered or in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 2 days. Wrap cut edges so they don't dry out.

title: Cantucci
summary: Twice-baked almond biscuits from Prato, made for dipping in vin santo.
steps: Heat the oven to 180°C. Mix the flour, sugar, baking powder, zest and salt, then add the eggs and almonds and bring it all together into a sticky dough.
With floured hands, shape two long logs on a lined baking tray and bake for 25 minutes, until golden and firm.
Cool for 10 minutes, then cut diagonally into slices about 1.5 cm thick with a serrated knife.
Lay the slices flat and bake for 10 minutes more, until dry and crisp. They keep for weeks in a tin.
keep: Store it in an airtight tin at room temperature. It keeps well for a couple of weeks.

title: Torta della nonna
summary: Grandma's cake: lemon custard in a shortcrust case, topped with pine nuts and icing sugar.
steps: Heat the milk with the lemon zest. In a pan, whisk the yolks, sugar and cornflour, pour in the hot milk and cook over low heat, whisking, until thick. Cover with cling film and cool.
Heat the oven to 180°C. Line a 24 cm tin with two thirds of the pastry and fill it with the cold custard.
Cover with the rest of the pastry, seal the edges well and scatter with pine nuts, pressing them in lightly.
Bake for about 45 minutes, until golden. Cool completely and dust with icing sugar before serving.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. Dairy-rich desserts shouldn't sit at room temperature for long, and some contain raw egg.

title: Bonet
summary: A Piedmontese baked pudding of chocolate, amaretti and caramel, served chilled.
steps: Melt 100 g of sugar in a dry pan over medium heat, swirling, until it turns a deep amber caramel. Pour it straight into a loaf tin and tilt to coat the bottom.
Whisk the eggs with the sugar, cocoa, crushed amaretti and rum, then whisk in the milk until smooth, and pour it over the caramel.
Set the tin in a larger dish, pour hot water around it to come halfway up, and bake at 160°C for about 50 minutes, until set.
Cool, then chill for at least 3 hours. Run a knife around the edge and turn it out onto a plate, so the caramel runs down the sides.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. Dairy-rich and set desserts shouldn't sit at room temperature for long.

title: Tortellini in brodo
summary: Tiny meat-filled pasta in a clear capon broth. The Christmas Day starter in Emilia-Romagna.
steps: Pour the broth into a pot and bring it slowly to a gentle simmer. Taste and season with salt: the broth is the star here, so it should taste rich and rounded.
Drop in the tortellini and stir once so they don't stick. Keep the broth at a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil, which can burst the delicate pasta.
Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, until the tortellini float to the surface and are tender.
Ladle the tortellini and plenty of broth into warm bowls and grate over Parmigiano at the table.
keep: This keeps well: cool it, then store it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. The flavour often gets even better overnight. Reheat gently in a pan until piping hot, adding a splash of water if it has thickened.

title: Risotto alla zucca
summary: Creamy pumpkin risotto with Parmigiano and crisp sage butter. Autumn in a bowl.
steps: Melt half the butter in a wide pan and soften the shallot for 3 minutes. Add the diced pumpkin and cook over medium heat, stirring, for about 10 minutes, until it starts to break down into a golden mush.
Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes to toast it, then pour in the wine and let it evaporate.

Add the hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring often and letting each ladle be absorbed before the next. Keep going for about 17 minutes, until the rice is tender with a little bite. The pumpkin melts into the rice and makes it creamy.
Meanwhile, fry the sage leaves in the remaining butter in a small pan until crisp and the butter smells nutty.
Take the risotto off the heat, stir in the Parmigiano and rest it for a minute. Serve topped with the crisp sage and a spoon of the sage butter.
keep: Cool risotto quickly, within an hour, then keep it covered in the fridge and eat it within 1 day. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of stock until piping hot, or roll it into balls, coat in breadcrumbs and fry as arancini.

title: Polenta e funghi
summary: Soft, buttery polenta topped with mushrooms sautéed with garlic and thyme. Mountain food for cold nights.
steps: Bring the salted water to the boil in a heavy pot. Pour in the polenta in a thin, steady stream, whisking all the time so no lumps form.
Turn the heat to low and cook, stirring often with a wooden spoon, for about 40 minutes, or as long as the packet says. It's ready when it's thick, smooth and pulls away from the sides of the pot.

Meanwhile, heat the oil in a wide pan over high heat and add the mushrooms in a single layer. Leave them to brown before stirring, then add the garlic and thyme and cook until golden. Season with salt and pepper.
Beat the butter and Parmigiano into the polenta until glossy.
Spoon the polenta onto warm plates, make a hollow in the middle and fill it with the mushrooms. Finish with chopped parsley.
keep: Keep the polenta and the mushrooms covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. Polenta sets firm as it cools: slice it and pan-fry or grill the slices, then top with the reheated mushrooms.

title: Insalata di rinforzo
summary: Naples' Christmas Eve cauliflower salad with pickled peppers, olives, anchovies and capers.
steps: Boil the cauliflower florets in salted water for about 6 minutes, so they're tender but still have some crunch. Drain and spread them out to cool.
Put the cauliflower in a large bowl with the pickled peppers, olives, capers and the anchovies torn into pieces.
Whisk the oil, vinegar and a pinch of salt and pour it over.
Toss gently and leave the salad for at least an hour, so the cauliflower soaks up the dressing. It's meant to sit and gets better over the holidays.
keep: This salad is meant to sit in its dressing. Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days and bring it to room temperature before serving.

title: Struffoli
summary: Tiny fried dough balls glazed in honey and heaped up with coloured sprinkles. A Neapolitan Christmas centrepiece.
steps: Mix the flour, eggs, soft butter, sugar, lemon zest and limoncello and knead into a soft, smooth dough. Wrap it and rest for 30 minutes.
Cut off pieces of dough and roll them into ropes about as thick as a pencil, then cut them into small pieces the size of a chickpea.
Heat the oil to 175°C and fry the struffoli in batches for 1 to 2 minutes, stirring, until golden. Drain them on kitchen paper.
Warm the honey gently in a wide pan until runny, take it off the heat and tip in the struffoli. Stir until every piece is coated.
Pile them onto a plate in a mound or a ring, using wet hands to shape them, and decorate with sprinkles and candied fruit. They hold together as the honey cools.
keep: Keep it covered or in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 2 days. Wrap cut edges so they don't dry out.

title: Castagnaccio
summary: A thin chestnut-flour cake with rosemary, pine nuts and raisins. Earthy, barely sweet and naturally gluten free.
steps: Heat the oven to 190°C and brush a 26 cm tin with olive oil.
Sift the chestnut flour into a bowl to remove any lumps, then whisk in the water and a pinch of salt little by little until you have a smooth batter, about as thick as pancake batter.
Pour it into the tin; it should be only about 1 cm deep. Scatter over the pine nuts, drained raisins and rosemary leaves and drizzle with oil.
Bake for about 35 minutes, until the top is dry and crackled. Serve warm or at room temperature.
keep: Keep it covered or in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 2 days. Wrap cut edges so they don't dry out.

title: Yosenabe
summary: A Japanese winter hot pot of chicken, fish, tofu and vegetables simmered at the table in light dashi.
ingredients: 300 g white fish fillet, in chunks
steps: Pour the dashi into a wide, shallow pot and season it with the soy sauce and mirin. Taste: it should be light and savoury.
Bring it to a simmer and add the chicken first, as it takes longest. Cook for 5 minutes, then add the cabbage, leeks and mushrooms.
Add the fish, prawns and tofu last and simmer gently, without stirring too much, until the fish turns opaque and the prawns pink.
Set the pot on the table, over a portable burner if you have one, and let everyone help themselves, adding more ingredients as you go.
keep: Seafood is best eaten the day it's cooked. If you have leftovers, cool them quickly, keep them covered in the fridge and eat them within 1 day, reheating gently.

title: Ravioli di stracciatella con pomodori e olive taggiasche
summary: Fresh egg pasta filled with creamy stracciatella, tossed with sautéed cherry tomatoes and small Ligurian olives.
steps: Pile the flour on a board, make a well in the middle and crack in the eggs. Beat them with a fork, gradually drawing in the flour, then knead for about 8 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap and rest for 30 minutes.
Drain the stracciatella well in a sieve, then mix it with the Parmigiano. A dry filling keeps the ravioli from going soggy.
Roll the dough into thin sheets. Place small spoonfuls of filling along one sheet, cover with a second, press around each mound to push out the air and cut into squares.
Warm the oil with the garlic in a wide pan, add the tomatoes and cook for about 5 minutes until they soften and release their juices. Add the olives.
Cook the ravioli in salted boiling water for about 3 minutes, lift them out with a slotted spoon and toss them gently in the sauce with torn basil.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Gnocchetti sardi con stracciatella, pomodorini e melanzane
summary: Ridged Sardinian pasta with roasted aubergine and cherry tomatoes, finished with a spoonful of cold stracciatella.
steps: Heat the oven to 210°C. Toss the aubergine and tomatoes with half the oil and some salt, spread them on a tray and roast for about 20 minutes, until the aubergine is golden and the tomatoes blister.
Cook the gnocchetti in salted boiling water until al dente, and keep a cup of the cooking water.
Warm the sliced garlic in the remaining oil, add the pasta, roasted vegetables and a splash of cooking water, and toss until the sauce turns creamy and coats the pasta.
Serve in bowls with spoonfuls of cold stracciatella and basil on top. The contrast of hot and cold is the point.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Polpette di melanzane con salsa tzatziki
summary: Crisp aubergine and pecorino balls served with a cool, garlicky yogurt sauce.
steps: Roast the whole aubergines at 200°C for about 35 minutes, until collapsed and soft. Halve them, scoop out the flesh and let it drain in a sieve for 15 minutes.
Mash the flesh with the breadcrumbs, pecorino, egg, half the garlic, parsley and salt. It should hold together when squeezed; add more breadcrumbs if it's too wet.
Shape small balls with wet hands and fry them in hot oil until golden, or bake them on an oiled tray at 200°C for about 20 minutes, turning once.
For the sauce, squeeze the grated cucumber dry and mix it with the yogurt, lemon juice, the rest of the garlic and salt. Serve the polpette warm with the cool sauce.
keep: These are best eaten fresh, while they're crisp. Leftovers keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 day. Reheat them on a tray in a hot oven (200°C) for 8 to 10 minutes to crisp them up again, rather than in the microwave.

title: Puccia salentina con polpette speziate
summary: Salento's soft, airy flatbread split open and filled with spiced meatballs, tomato and rocket.
steps: Mix the flour, yeast, warm water and salt and knead into a soft, slightly sticky dough. Cover and leave it to rise for about an hour, until doubled.
Divide into 4, shape round flat breads about 1 cm thick and rest them for 20 minutes. Bake at 230°C for about 12 minutes, until puffed and pale golden.
Meanwhile, mix the beef with the cumin, paprika, egg, breadcrumbs and salt, roll into small balls and fry them in a pan until browned and cooked through.
Split the warm breads open and fill them with the meatballs, tomato slices and rocket.
keep: Keep the filling in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days, separate from the bread or tortillas and the fresh toppings. Reheat the filling in a hot pan and warm the bread just before serving.

title: Torta salata con salmone e mozzarella
summary: A savoury puff pastry tart with smoked salmon, mozzarella and a creamy egg filling.
steps: Heat the oven to 190°C and line a tart tin with the puff pastry, letting it come up the sides. Prick the base with a fork.
Scatter the diced mozzarella and torn smoked salmon evenly over the base.
Whisk the eggs with the cream, chopped dill and black pepper. The salmon is salty, so add only a little salt.
Pour the mixture over the filling and bake for about 35 minutes, until set in the middle and golden on top. Let it rest for 10 minutes before slicing.
keep: Seafood is best eaten the day it's cooked. If you have leftovers, cool them quickly, keep them covered in the fridge and eat them within 1 day, reheating gently.

title: Cheesecake al pandoro con mandorle e crumble
summary: A no-bake cheesecake on a pandoro base, topped with toasted almonds and biscuit crumble. Good for leftover Christmas pandoro.
steps: Line the base and sides of a 22 cm springform tin with slices of pandoro, pressing them together so there are no gaps.
Whip the cream to soft peaks. In another bowl, beat the cream cheese with the icing sugar and lemon zest until smooth, then fold in the whipped cream.
Spread the filling over the pandoro and smooth the top.
Rub the biscuits with the melted butter into crumbs and toast them in a dry pan for a few minutes until golden. Cool.
Scatter the crumble and toasted almonds over the cheesecake and chill for at least 4 hours before releasing it from the tin.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. Dairy-rich and set desserts shouldn't sit at room temperature for long.

title: Lasagne cicoria e pecorino
summary: White lasagne layered with bitter chicory, béchamel and sharp pecorino.
steps: Boil the chicory in salted water for about 8 minutes, drain, squeeze out the water and chop it roughly. Sauté it with the garlic and oil for a few minutes.
Heat the oven to 190°C. Spread a thin layer of béchamel in a baking dish.
Layer pasta sheets, chicory, béchamel and pecorino, and repeat about five times.
Finish with béchamel and a good handful of pecorino, and bake for about 35 minutes, until golden and bubbling. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. It often slices even better the next day. Reheat portions in the oven at 180°C, covered with foil, for about 20 minutes, until hot in the middle.

title: Crostata con confettura di pesche e mandorle
summary: An almond shortcrust tart filled with peach jam and scattered with flaked almonds.
steps: Rub the cold butter into the flour and ground almonds until it looks like breadcrumbs, then add the sugar and egg and bring it together into a dough. Wrap and chill for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 180°C. Roll out two thirds of the pastry and line a 24 cm tart tin.
Spread the peach jam over the base. Roll out the rest of the pastry, cut strips and lay them over the top in a lattice, then scatter with flaked almonds.
Bake for about 35 minutes, until golden. Cool completely before slicing so the jam sets.
keep: Keep it covered or in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 2 days. Wrap cut edges so they don't dry out.

title: Spaghetti alla crudaiola con Brie e pomodoro fresco
summary: A no-cook summer sauce of raw tomatoes, basil and melting Brie, tossed with hot spaghetti.
steps: Dice the tomatoes and put them in a large bowl with the crushed garlic, torn basil, oil and a good pinch of salt. Leave them for 15 minutes, so the tomatoes release their juices into the oil.
Cook the spaghetti in salted boiling water until al dente.
Drain the pasta and tip it straight into the bowl with the cubed Brie, tossing well. The heat of the pasta melts the cheese into the raw sauce.
Fish out the garlic clove and serve straight away.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Pasta e broccoli al forno con scamorza affumicata
summary: Baked pasta with broccoli and smoky scamorza, crisp on top and creamy underneath.
steps: Bring a pot of salted water to the boil and cook the broccoli for 4 minutes. Lift it out, then cook the pasta in the same water until just short of al dente.
Warm the oil with the garlic and chili in a pan, add the broccoli and cook for a few minutes, crushing it slightly with a spoon so it becomes almost a sauce.
Heat the oven to 200°C. Mix the pasta with the broccoli, béchamel and diced scamorza and spread it in a baking dish. Scatter Parmigiano over the top.
Bake for about 20 minutes, until golden and crisp on top and melting underneath.
keep: Keep it covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. It often slices even better the next day. Reheat portions in the oven at 180°C, covered with foil, for about 20 minutes, until hot in the middle.

title: Linguine all'ortolana
summary: Linguine with a garden's worth of sautéed vegetables: courgette, pepper, aubergine and cherry tomatoes.
steps: Dice all the vegetables into small, even pieces so they cook at the same speed.
Warm the oil in a large pan and cook the aubergine and pepper for about 8 minutes, until soft and golden. Add the courgette and garlic, then the tomatoes, and cook for 5 minutes more.
Cook the linguine until al dente and add them to the pan with a splash of cooking water. Toss well over the heat.
Finish with torn basil and a drizzle of olive oil.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Panzanella estiva di fagioli
summary: A summer bread salad bulked up with cannellini beans, cherry tomatoes and red onion.
steps: Tear the bread into chunks, sprinkle it with a little water and the vinegar, and leave it for about 5 minutes to soften.
Halve the tomatoes and slice the onion and cucumber.
Put everything in a big bowl with the beans, oil, salt and torn basil and toss gently with your hands.
Rest for 15 minutes before serving so the bread soaks up the juices.
keep: Salads are best fresh. To keep some, store the undressed ingredients in the fridge for up to 1 day and dress them just before eating. Keep crunchy things like toasted bread or nuts separate until the last minute.

title: Tagliolini al salmone, whisky e burro al tartufo
summary: Fine egg ribbons with smoked salmon flambéed in whisky and a knob of truffle butter.
steps: Melt a little of the truffle butter in a wide pan and soften the chopped shallot for 2 minutes. Add the salmon strips and stir for a minute.
Pour in the whisky, standing back, and let it bubble until the alcohol has evaporated.
Add the cream and simmer for 2 minutes, until slightly thickened.
Cook the tagliolini for about 2 minutes, then lift them into the sauce with the rest of the truffle butter and a splash of cooking water. Toss gently and finish with chives.
keep: Seafood is best eaten the day it's cooked. If you have leftovers, cool them quickly, keep them covered in the fridge and eat them within 1 day, reheating gently.

title: Spaghetti con crema di piselli, pecorino e pistacchi
summary: A bright green pea cream with pecorino, finished with crunchy chopped pistachios.
steps: Warm the oil in a pan and soften the shallot for 3 minutes. Add the peas and a ladle of water and simmer for about 8 minutes, until tender.
Blend the peas with half the pecorino, the mint and enough cooking liquid to make a smooth, bright green cream.
Cook the spaghetti until al dente and toss them with the pea cream and a little pasta water until glossy.
Serve topped with the chopped pistachios and the rest of the pecorino.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Frittata di zucca e patate
summary: A thick frittata with soft pumpkin and potato, scented with rosemary.
steps: Warm the oil in a 24 cm non-stick pan and add the pumpkin, potato and onion with a pinch of salt. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for about 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until soft.
Beat the eggs with the Parmigiano, chopped rosemary and salt, and pour them over the vegetables.
Cover and cook on low heat for about 8 minutes, until almost set.
Flip the frittata with the help of a plate and cook for 2 minutes more. Serve warm or at room temperature.
keep: Keep them covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat on a tray in a hot oven (220°C) for about 10 minutes so they crisp up again; the microwave makes them soft.

title: Hamburger di lenticchie con cicoria e pecorino
summary: Hearty lentil burgers with bitter sautéed chicory and shavings of pecorino.
steps: Mash the lentils roughly with a fork, then mix in the breadcrumbs, egg, cumin and salt. Shape four patties and chill them for 15 minutes so they hold together.
Boil the chicory for about 6 minutes, squeeze out the water and sauté it with the garlic and a little oil.
Fry the burgers in the remaining oil over medium heat for about 4 minutes per side, until crisp outside.
Toast the buns and fill them with the burgers, chicory and shaved pecorino.
keep: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat gently until piping hot all the way through, covered so it doesn't dry out.

title: Pasta con lo sgombro
summary: A quick pantry pasta with mackerel, cherry tomatoes, capers and toasted breadcrumbs.
steps: Warm a spoonful of the oil from the mackerel tin in a wide pan with the garlic and chili, then add the tomatoes and cook for about 5 minutes, until soft.
Flake in the mackerel and add the capers, stirring gently so the fish stays in pieces.
Cook the pasta until al dente and toss it into the pan with a splash of cooking water.
Serve topped with toasted breadcrumbs and parsley, which add crunch in place of cheese.
keep: Seafood is best eaten the day it's cooked. If you have leftovers, cool them quickly, keep them covered in the fridge and eat them within 1 day, reheating gently.

title: Risotto con pomodorini arrosto, alici e stracciatella
summary: Creamy risotto topped with sweet roasted tomatoes, salty anchovies and cold stracciatella.
steps: Toss the cherry tomatoes with the oil and some salt and roast at 200°C for about 25 minutes, until soft and caramelised.
Soften the shallot in a little oil, add the rice and toast it for 2 minutes, then pour in the wine and let it evaporate.
Add the hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring often, for about 17 minutes, until the rice is tender and creamy.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the butter.
Spoon into bowls and top with the roasted tomatoes, anchovy fillets and a spoonful of cold stracciatella.
keep: Cool risotto quickly, within an hour, then keep it covered in the fridge and eat it within 1 day. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of stock until piping hot, or roll it into balls, coat in breadcrumbs and fry as arancini.

title: Tagliolini al tartufo, crema di cavolfiore e burrata affumicata
summary: Tagliolini in a silky cauliflower cream with truffle butter, crowned with smoked burrata.
steps: Simmer the cauliflower and shallot in the stock for about 15 minutes, until very soft, then blend until silky smooth.
Cook the tagliolini for about 2 minutes, drain and toss them in the warm cauliflower cream with the truffle butter.
Divide between plates and tear the smoked burrata over the top.
Finish with a twist of black pepper.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Mozzarelle in carrozza
summary: Mozzarella sandwiches dipped in egg and fried until golden, with a molten, stretchy middle.
ingredients: 250 g mozzarella, sliced and patted dry
steps: Make four sandwiches with the bread and mozzarella. The cheese should be well drained and patted dry, or it will make the bread soggy. Press the edges firmly together.
Dip each sandwich in flour on both sides, then in the eggs beaten with the milk, letting them soak for a few seconds.
Heat the oil in a frying pan and fry the sandwiches over medium heat until golden on both sides and the cheese inside has melted.
Drain on kitchen paper, sprinkle with salt and eat hot.
keep: These are best eaten fresh, while they're crisp. Leftovers keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 day. Reheat them on a tray in a hot oven (200°C) for 8 to 10 minutes to crisp them up again, rather than in the microwave.

title: Spaghetti al cavolo nero con burrata
summary: Spaghetti in a garlicky blended cavolo nero sauce, topped with creamy burrata.
steps: Strip the leaves of the cavolo nero from the tough stalks and boil them in salted water for about 5 minutes.
Blend the leaves with the garlic, oil, Parmigiano and a little cooking water into a smooth, deep green sauce.
Cook the spaghetti in the same water until al dente and toss them with the sauce.
Serve topped with torn burrata and a pinch of chili flakes.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Cous cous di verdure e frutta secca su gazpacho
summary: Vegetable couscous with almonds and raisins, served on a cold, tangy tomato gazpacho.
steps: Put the couscous in a bowl, pour over the boiling salted water, cover and leave for 5 minutes. Fluff it up with a fork.
Sauté the diced courgette and pepper in a little oil until just tender, then mix them into the couscous with the almonds and raisins.
Blend the tomatoes, cucumber, garlic, vinegar and most of the oil until smooth, season with salt and chill.
Pour the cold gazpacho into shallow bowls and pile the couscous in the middle.
keep: Salads are best fresh. To keep some, store the undressed ingredients in the fridge for up to 1 day and dress them just before eating. Keep crunchy things like toasted bread or nuts separate until the last minute.

title: Insalatona fresca con noci
summary: A big crunchy salad with apple, fennel, greens and walnuts in a lemon and honey dressing.
steps: Slice the apple and fennel as thinly as you can.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for a few minutes until fragrant.
Whisk the lemon juice, oil, honey and a pinch of salt into a dressing.
Toss the leaves, apple and fennel with the dressing and top with crumbled goat's cheese and walnuts.
keep: Salads are best fresh. To keep some, store the undressed ingredients in the fridge for up to 1 day and dress them just before eating. Keep crunchy things like toasted bread or nuts separate until the last minute.

title: Tortino al cioccolato con cuore morbido e torrone
summary: Individual chocolate puddings with a molten heart and chopped nougat. A good use for leftover torrone.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C. Butter four ramekins and dust them with cocoa so the puddings turn out easily.
Melt the chocolate and butter together. Whisk the eggs, yolks and sugar until thick and pale, fold in the chocolate, then the flour.
Half-fill the ramekins, add a few pieces of torrone to each, and top with the remaining mixture.
Bake for 10 to 11 minutes, until the edges are firm but the centre still wobbles. Turn them out straight away and serve warm.
keep: Best eaten warm, straight from the oven, while the centre is molten. You can fill the ramekins up to a day ahead and keep them in the fridge, then bake them just before serving, adding a minute to the time.

title: Linguine con peperoni arrosto, capperi e olive
summary: Linguine with sweet roasted peppers, capers and black olives.
steps: Roast the whole peppers at 220°C for about 25 minutes, turning once, until blistered and soft. Put them in a bowl, cover and let them steam for 10 minutes, then peel, seed and slice them.
Warm the garlic in the oil, add the peppers, capers and olives and cook for a few minutes.
Cook the linguine until al dente and toss them in the pan with a little pasta water.
Finish with chopped parsley.
keep: Keep it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of water to loosen the sauce, or let it come to room temperature if it's an oil-based dish.

title: Risotto al burro con arancia, Parmigiano e bottarga
summary: A buttery white risotto lifted with orange zest and finished with grated bottarga.
steps: Soften the shallot in a little of the butter, add the rice and toast it for 2 minutes, then add the wine and let it evaporate.
Add the hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring often, for about 17 minutes, until the rice is tender.
Take it off the heat and beat in the rest of the butter, the Parmigiano, the finely grated orange zest and a splash of orange juice. Taste: the orange should be fresh, not overpowering.
Serve with bottarga grated over the top at the table.
keep: Cool risotto quickly, within an hour, then keep it covered in the fridge and eat it within 1 day. Reheat it in a pan with a splash of stock until piping hot, or roll it into balls, coat in breadcrumbs and fry as arancini.

title: Patate dolci croccanti con due salse
summary: Oven-crisp sweet potato wedges with two dips: smoky paprika mayonnaise and herby Greek yogurt.
